The vague tool matched "tell me about" better than the precise one, so the model picked it. Overlapping, vague descriptions cause selection errors that look like model mistakes but are tool design mistakes.
Which tool the model picks first will vary between runs; the token overhead will not.

checkpoint.a: Your application does. The model returns a tool_use block naming a tool and its input, and your harness decides whether to run it, runs it, and sends back a tool_result. That is why validation, permissions and side-effect controls belong in harness code, not in the prompt.

checkpoint.q: Why is a tool description a prompt?
checkpoint.a: The API renders tool names, descriptions and schemas into the model's context, and the model chooses which tool to call and with what arguments by reading them. A vague description therefore produces wrong selections and badly formed inputs, exactly like a vague instruction. The docs call detailed descriptions the most important factor in tool performance.

checkpoint.q: What do you return when a tool throws, and why not just raise?
checkpoint.a: Return a tool_result for that tool_use_id with is_error: true and a message that says what went wrong and how to fix it. Raising ends the loop and leaves the tool_use unanswered, while an actionable error lets the model correct itself on the next turn, as the failure cell showed.

checkpoint.q: Why do 40 tools make selection worse rather than better?
checkpoint.a: More tools means more overlapping descriptions for the model to choose between, so ambiguity and wrong picks increase, and every definition is paid for in input tokens on every request. Consolidating related operations, namespacing names, and loading rarely used tools on demand (for example with tool search) keep the choice small and clear.
